title: Money
subtitle: overdraft, mortgage, income, VAT
summary: Handle the language of money - current and savings accounts, loans, mortgages and overdrafts, income and outgoings, and the main kinds of tax.

lesson.heading: Banking words from the advertisements
rows: the account you use for most everyday business
the percentage the bank pays you based on how much you have in your account
permission to have a negative amount of money in your account
the maximum amount of money you may spend on your card
as good as or better than other banks
a loan used usually to buy a house
money you pay before buying something to show you really want to buy it
payments that reduce the amount you owe

lesson.heading: Borrowing and raising money
lesson.text: If you are **short of cash** you may need a **loan**. To **raise** money is to find it; to **finance** something is to find the money needed to pay for it. To **consolidate** your debts is to join them together to make one payment.

examples.text: Need to **raise** money for that round-the-world trip? Look for a loan with **competitive** interest rates.
I need to buy a car, but I'm not sure how I'm going to **finance** it.
**Consolidate** all your cards and debts into one convenient **payment**.

lesson.heading: Money in and money out

left.label: Coming in
examples: I have a steady **income** now, which is great.
**income** = money coming in regularly, in a way that does not change much
My account is **in credit** at the beginning of the month.
**in credit** = has a positive amount of money in it

right.label: Going out
examples: My **outgoings** are quite low and I don't have any major **expenses**.
**outgoings** = money you pay each month, e.g. rent or the cost of running a car
By the end of the month my account is always **overdrawn**.
I hate being **in the red** and the banks all **charge interest** on overdrafts.

lesson.note: In the red is informal for having a negative amount of money in your account.

lesson.heading: Bank services
lesson.text: You can pay bills by **direct debit**, so money is taken automatically from your account. A **savings account** is where you put money you do not immediately need, and you can **transfer** money from one account to another.

examples.text: Paying by direct debit means I have a good **credit rating**, so I can borrow money if I need to.
examples.note: credit rating = a bank's judgement of how likely you are to pay back money you borrow

examples.text: The bank **debits** your account for the necessary sums; if it puts money in, it **credits** your account.
I use **online banking** most of the time and only go to the bank to use the **cash machine**.
I try not to go over my **overdraft limit**.

lesson.heading: Public finance: kinds of tax
rows: money people get from people who have died
lesson.note: Airports usually have **duty-free** shops, where you do not pay this tax.

lesson.text: A deposit is money paid up front to show you really want to buy; a repayment is money paid back to reduce a loan - don't mix them up.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with its definition.

pairs.right: money that is charged on a loan
a loan to buy a house or flat
an account with a negative sum of money in it
an account for money you don't need immediately
a payment taken automatically from an account

exercises.prompt: What do we call each of these?

pairs.left: the tax you pay on imported goods
a shop at an airport where you don't pay tax
a tax added to most goods and services
a tax on money paid if someone dies
the tax companies pay on their profits
the tax taken out of your salary

exercises.prompt: Nico owes his brother 5,000 euros and he borrowed 10,000 euros to buy a car. Nico has ___ totalling 15,000 euros.
exercises.explanation: Debts are sums of money you owe.

exercises.prompt: Misha spent 6,000 euros on her card; the bank said she'd spent 1,000 too much. Her credit ___ was 5,000 euros.
exercises.explanation: Your credit limit is the maximum you may spend on the card.

exercises.prompt: Newbank's interest rates are similar to other banks' rates and sometimes better. Newbank's rates are ___.
exercises.explanation: Competitive means as good as or better than other banks.

exercises.prompt: Before she bought her new car, Alice paid 500 pounds to the dealer. She paid a ___ of 500 pounds.
exercises.explanation: A deposit is money paid before buying, to show you really want to buy.

exercises.prompt: If customers need more money than is in their account, the bank can offer them an overdraft ___.
exercises.explanation: An overdraft facility is permission to have a negative amount in your account.

exercises.prompt: Harry sold his car and got a part-time job. He was trying to ___ money for his trip to Africa.
exercises.explanation: To raise money is to find it, often from several sources.

exercises.prompt: Harry needed the money to ___ his trip to Africa.
exercises.explanation: To finance something is to find the money needed to pay for it.

exercises.prompt: You only need one credit card. You can combine all the sums you owe into one ___.
exercises.explanation: Consolidating debts turns several debts into one convenient payment.

exercises.prompt: The bank offers mortgages with ___ over 30 years.
exercises.explanation: Repayments are the payments that reduce the amount you owe.

exercises.prompt: If your account is overdrawn, what is true?
options: You have a negative amount of money in it.
You have a large positive balance.
The bank pays you extra interest.
exercises.explanation: Overdrawn means there is a negative amount in the account - informally, you are in the red.

exercises.prompt: If your bank debited your account for 500 euros, what has happened?
options: You have less money - the bank has taken it out.
You have more money - the bank has put it in.
Your credit limit has gone up.
exercises.explanation: A bank debits your account when it takes money out and credits it when it puts money in.

exercises.prompt: If you have a good credit rating, what will you find easier to do?
exercises.explanation: A good credit rating means banks feel confident you will pay the money back.

exercises.statement: Zara's account is in credit, so she probably has a positive amount of money in it.
exercises.explanation: Correct - in credit is the opposite of overdrawn.

exercises.statement: Bob doesn't have a steady income and his outgoings are very high, so he probably feels secure.
exercises.explanation: False - he probably feels insecure, because his income may go up and down and may not cover his outgoings.

exercises.prompt: Sort these into money coming in and money going out.
